title: Trump Signs New Executive Orders to Restrict Birthright Citizenship After Supreme Court Rebuke
excerpt: The president's narrower approach targets 'birth tourism' and children of 'alien enemies,' weeks after the court struck down his broader ban as unconstitutional.
body:
• President Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday targeting birthright citizenship, weeks after the Supreme Court struck down his broader attempt in a 6-3 ruling.
  • The first order expands the definition of those ineligible for birthright citizenship to include children of 'alien enemies,' foreign terrorist organization members, and foreign government operatives.
  • The second order directs agencies to crack down on 'birth tourism' — foreigners entering the U.S. specifically to give birth on American soil.
  • Legal experts expect swift court challenges, given the Supreme Court's recent forceful defense of 14th Amendment protections.

President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday in a renewed attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in the United States, just five weeks after the Supreme Court decisively rejected his earlier, broader effort as unconstitutional.

The new orders take a narrower approach than last year's sweeping directive, which sought to deny citizenship to all children born in the U.S. to non-citizen parents. That executive order was struck down on June 30 when the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that it violated the 14th Amendment's guarantee of citizenship to anyone born on American soil.

What the New Orders Do

The first executive order expands the categories of individuals whose U.S.-born children would be deemed ineligible for birthright citizenship. According to White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the order targets children born to 'alien enemies,' members of foreign terrorist organizations, and people who 'lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments.'

The administration argues these categories 'do not fall within the rule of birthright citizenship as announced by the Supreme Court,' citing narrow exceptions the court has historically recognized for children born to diplomats and enemies during hostile occupation.

The second order focuses on so-called birth tourism, directing the State Department and Department of Homeland Security to deny visas and take other steps to prevent individuals from entering the country 'for the purpose of engaging in birth tourism.'

"That practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned. No one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a visa for this fraudulent purpose."

— Stephen Miller, White House Deputy Chief of Staff

Context and Background

'We had a very unfortunate decision in the Supreme Court concerning birthright, so we're making adjustments,' Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, according to USA Today.

The June 30 ruling in Trump v. Barbara was a landmark moment. Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for a five-justice majority, declared that 'citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community.' Justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred in part, concluding the original order was barred by federal law rather than the Constitution itself.

Three conservative justices — Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch — dissented. Thomas argued the majority had created 'a constitutional right to citizenship for the children of all foreign birth tourists and illegal aliens.' Alito, in a solo dissent, warned that the ruling conferred citizenship on 'virtually everyone who happens to be born in this country.'

Legal Outlook

Legal scholars and civil liberties organizations are expected to challenge the new orders swiftly. The American Civil Liberties Union, which successfully challenged the first executive order, has called birthright citizenship 'foundational to who we are as a nation,' according to USA Today.

Miller's assertion that the new categories fall outside the court's ruling may face skepticism, given the breadth of the majority opinion. U.S. law already prohibits obtaining a visa 'for the primary purpose of obtaining U.S. citizenship for a child by giving birth in the United States,' making the practical impact of the birth tourism order unclear, as CNN reported.

The Center for Immigration Studies, which favors lower immigration levels, estimated in 2020 that between 20,000 and 25,000 mothers came to the U.S. for birth tourism annually — a fraction of the 3.6 million total births recorded in 2025, according to Reuters.

Impact on the Indian Diaspora

The orders carry particular significance for the Indian American community. Hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals hold temporary work visas in the United States, and many have U.S.-born children whose citizenship has been automatic under longstanding constitutional interpretation. While the new orders do not directly target this population, the expanding definitions of ineligibility and the administration's willingness to test new constitutional boundaries have heightened anxiety among immigrant communities.

Immigration attorneys say the broader concern is the precedent these orders set — that executive action can chip away at birthright protections even after the Supreme Court has ruled on the matter.

What's Next

The executive orders are expected to face immediate legal challenges. Federal courts blocked Trump's first attempt within days of its signing in January 2025, and the case ultimately reached the Supreme Court within 18 months. If history is any guide, the new orders may follow a similar trajectory — though the narrower framing could make them harder to challenge on the same constitutional grounds.

Meanwhile, Republican Representative John McGuire has introduced the Birthright Citizenship Clarification Act in Congress, seeking to codify restrictions through legislation rather than executive action alone.
nri_angle: Indian Americans on H-1B and other temporary visas whose U.S.-born children hold automatic citizenship could face uncertainty as the administration tests new limits on birthright protections.
